name: Forward head posture exercises

card.summary: Neck-strengthening and chin-tuck style routines for forward head posture; studied for neck pain, with community debate over whether they help or hurt the profile.
card.aka: Chin tucks, neck strengthening, tech neck exercises
card.note: Studies link forward head posture and neck pain, but the association is not uniform and cosmetic effects are unstudied.

quick.overview:
Forward head posture (FHP, also called nerd neck or tech neck) is when the head sits ahead of the shoulders. Exercise routines for it usually aim to strengthen the deep neck flexors and upper back and stretch tight muscles at the neck and chest.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed both as a way to improve profile and posture and as something that might make a recessed chin look worse once the head is pulled back. Research focuses on neck pain and headache, not looks.
quick.mechanism: FHP is quantified by the craniovertebral angle. Exercise programmes target the deep cervical flexors and scapular muscles, and a trial found neck exercises improved the ability of people with chronic neck pain to hold an upright posture during a task.
quick.risks: Exercise itself is generally low risk, but nothing shows that exercise permanently changes head position or appearance. Evidence linking FHP to pain is mixed, with a meta-analysis finding an association in adults but not adolescents.

lead: Forward head posture (FHP) is a posture in which the head sits forward of the shoulders, often accompanied by rounded shoulders and increased upper-back curvature. It is commonly called text neck, tech neck or nerd neck, and is measured clinically with the craniovertebral angle.[1][2][3] Exercises for it typically aim to strengthen the deep neck flexors and shoulder-blade retractors and to stretch tight neck and chest muscles.[3]

People work on it to look more upright and balanced: pulling the head back over the shoulders changes the silhouette in profile, reduces the hunched look of the upper back and neck, and practitioners describe a longer-looking neck. In looksmaxxing communities the exercise most often associated with it is the chin tuck, frequently paired with weighted neck curls, and users also connect it to the position of the hyoid bone and the submental area.[18][19]

Research has examined the association of FHP with neck pain and headache and tested exercise regimens in people with neck pain.[4][5][6] A systematic review and meta-analysis found that adults with neck pain had greater forward head posture than adults without it, a difference not seen in adolescents.[7] Some forum users argue that correction can make a recessed chin look weaker; no published study has examined these appearance claims.[15]

chain: Strengthen deep neck flexors and upper-back muscles; stretch tight neck and chest muscles
Head is carried closer to over the shoulders and the upper back stands straighter
More upright side profile and a longer-looking neck, depending on individual structure
angle.text: Programmes of chin tucks, scapular and thoracic work are used to bring the head back over the shoulders so the profile looks more upright. How this shows up in the face and jawline varies between people and is debated on forums.

paras: Wikipedia describes FHP as a hunched, kyphotic upper spine with the head carried forward, common among people who spend long hours at devices and in certain occupations, and lists dentists, surgeons, hairdressers, nurses, chefs, teachers and students among those affected by prolonged hunching.[3] When the head sits forward the ear lobe lies in front of a vertical line through the shoulder.[3]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes measurement by the craniovertebral angle, taken between a horizontal line at the seventh cervical vertebra and a line to the ear, with values below 50 degrees taken to indicate FHP and values under 30 degrees called severe.[1] It also describes the upper crossed pattern, which combines tight upper trapezius, levator scapulae and pectoral muscles with weak deep neck flexors.[1][16]

Text neck and tech neck refer to the association with phones, tablets and laptops, while nerd neck is the forum and popular term. Combined with rounded shoulders, FHP is called upper crossed syndrome on Wikipedia.[3][16] The article that carries the term carries maintenance tags noting that several of its statements need stronger sources.[16]

Wikipedia repeats a figure that about 10 pounds of load is added to the cervical spine per inch of forward head position, attributing it to a 2014 paper by Hansraj in Surgical Technology International, and says the derivation is not explained on the page.[3] Grokipedia gives modelled loads rising from about 10 to 12 pounds in neutral posture to about 27, 40 and 60 pounds at 15, 30 and 60 degrees of flexion.[1]

Wikipedia associates FHP with prolonged hunching over laptops, tablets and phones, and notes that conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis, Parkinson's disease and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome can cause similar thoracic kyphosis.[3] It states that the attribution of rising neck pain to device use is an inference from timing rather than a demonstrated causal finding.[3]

Prevalence estimates vary by method. Grokipedia cites reviews from 2020 to 2024 giving figures between about 66 and 80 percent across populations and notes that differences between self-report and clinical measurement drive variation.[1] Wikipedia cites Fejer and colleagues (2006) for adult neck pain prevalence of 5.9 to 22.2 percent.[3]

Programmes commonly described include strengthening the deep neck flexors and mid and lower back muscles, stretching the upper trapezius and chest, breaks from sustained postures, and ergonomic changes.[3] Thoracic manipulation has also been studied for neck pain, and Wikipedia cites Cleland and colleagues (2005), a randomised trial in which thoracic manipulation reduced neck pain immediately.[3]

Grokipedia lists a wider menu: chin tucks including wall-assisted and supine versions, wall stands with heels, buttocks, shoulder blades and head against a wall, shoulder-blade squeezes, doorway chest stretches, wall angels, band pull-aparts, W and Y raises, prone neck lifts, isometric neck presses and thoracic extension over a chair or foam roller.[1] It describes typical programmes of 8 to 12 weeks, three to five times weekly, for 20 to 30 minutes.[1]

A trial of 58 people compared two neck-exercise regimens for the ability of people with chronic neck pain to maintain an upright cervical and thoracic posture during a distracting task.[5] Ergonomic suggestions on Grokipedia include screens at or slightly below eye level, breaks every 20 to 30 minutes, and cervical pillows.[1]

sections.h: Chin tucks and neck curls in looksmaxxing
paras: On looksmax.org the chin tuck and the weighted neck curl are treated as a pair. A recurring thread format asks whether they are 'cope or real'; one poster says they have done three sets of 20 and noticed a small change, and a reply says the exercises are not cope unless the user expects to become a 'chad', while another poster says the aim is to 'raise hyoid'.[18]

A before-and-after post says the face and posture looked different with equal weight and facial fat; the poster describes adding weight with towels to chin tucks, and replies attribute the difference to raising the hyoid bone and say users have 'known they work'.[19] A further thread claims that chin-tuck positioning makes the voice deeper and more resonant, with the poster crediting a voice therapist's exercise for puberphonia.[20] Other threads ask how to perform chin tucks efficiently, whether they widen the jaw, and why the neck hurts during them.[21][22]

Counter-views in the same community hold that pulling the head back exposes a recessed chin and makes the profile look weaker.[15] No published study has tested whether chin tucks or neck curls raise the hyoid bone, change submental appearance or alter jaw shape.

Forum users discuss FHP alongside mewing and tongue posture, neck training, and posture correctors. Wikipedia's neck-pain treatment list also includes Pilates, the Alexander Technique and yoga as general approaches, which have their own entries or are covered in the wider posture category.[3]

Forum posts ask whether neck pain during chin tucks is normal.[22] Grokipedia says throat discomfort and pain on swallowing associated with neck tension require medical evaluation to rule out other causes.[1] Wikipedia notes that FHP can occur with conditions such as Parkinson's disease and ankylosing spondylitis, which clinicians evaluate separately.[3]

A cross-sectional study of 62 people with neck pain and 52 without examined head posture measured by the craniovertebral angle in relation to pain and disability. It found a smaller angle in the neck-pain group, and a moderate correlation between smaller angle and greater disability.[4] Older studies reported differences in head posture and upper cervical flexor performance in people with cervical headache and in tension-type headache and migraine.[8][9][10]

A 2007 randomised trial in Physical Therapy by Falla and colleagues enrolled 58 adults with chronic neck pain and 10 controls. Over a 10-minute computer task, the neck-pain group showed a larger forward shift of the head (4.4 degrees versus 2.2 degrees in controls); after six weeks, the group that did craniocervical flexor training showed a significant reduction in that forward shift.[5]

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis in Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine included 15 cross-sectional studies. Adults with neck pain showed greater forward head posture than those without (mean difference 4.84), while adolescents showed no significant difference. In adults, forward head posture was correlated with pain intensity and disability, and the authors identified age as an important confounder.[7]

Grokipedia reports a 2024 meta-analysis of 22 studies with 903 participants in which exercise-based programmes improved craniovertebral angle by a pooled 3.90 degrees.[1] An observational study compared neck and shoulder postures in symptomatic and asymptomatic office workers, and an earlier study examined postural abnormalities and pain in healthy adults of two age groups.[11][12] A 2005 study examined the relationship between cervical lordosis and neck complaints.[6]
No studies found testing whether FHP exercises change facial appearance, jaw or chin profile.

lore.intro: Forum discussion of forward head posture splits between those who treat it as a flaw to fix with chin tucks and neck curls and those who question whether fixing it helps looks.[13][14][15][18]

claims.claim: Forward head posture causes problems throughout the body.
claims.believers: A thread presents FHP as harming the whole body and says it feels natural after a period of good posture [14].
claims.experts: Studies associate FHP with neck pain and headache in some groups, though a meta-analysis found the link in adults but not adolescents [3][7].

claims.claim: Fixing forward head posture makes a recessed chin look worse.
claims.believers: A user says a chin tuck leaves him with almost no visible chin and asks whether correcting posture is worthwhile [15].
claims.experts: No published study has examined how head position changes chin appearance in the context of exercise.

claims.claim: Forward head posture may affect maxillary growth.
claims.believers: A user wonders whether years of gaming with forward head posture affected his forward-grown maxilla [13].
claims.experts: No studies on head posture and maxillary growth have been published.

claims.claim: Models and actors have forward head posture, so correcting it may be unnecessary.
claims.believers: A thread asks whether correction is 'cope', with a reply saying they pose that way for photos [13].
claims.experts: No study found testing attractiveness ratings of head posture.

claims.claim: Chin tucks and neck curls raise the hyoid bone and improve the jaw and neck area.
claims.believers: Posters recommend three sets of 20 chin tucks plus neck curls to 'raise hyoid', and share before-and-after photos attributing a changed look to weighted chin tucks.[18][19]
claims.experts: No published study has measured hyoid position or submental appearance after chin tucks; trials of neck exercise address craniocervical flexor function and head position in people with neck pain.[5]

claims.claim: Chin tucks make the voice deeper and more resonant.
claims.believers: One user reports a deeper, more resonant voice in a chin-tuck position and describes a voice-therapist exercise used for puberphonia.[20]
claims.experts: No studies found testing chin tucks as a voice-deepening method.

claims.claim: Weighted neck work corrects posture permanently.
claims.believers: A poster describes adding weight to chin tucks and reports improving posture day by day.[19]
claims.experts: A 2007 trial found craniocervical flexor training reduced forward head shift during a computer task over six weeks; long-term appearance outcomes have not been tracked.[5]
